strengths: The paper addresses a relevant instruction-tuning problem with a straightforward recipe: partition examples by training confidence and combine hidden-state Mixup with next-token prediction. The core algorithm and main training hyperparameters are clearly described.

The empirical coverage is substantial. Table 1 reports consistent improvements across seven model–dataset combinations, including three model families and datasets approaching one million examples. Medical QA experiments provide additional evidence beyond instruction-following judges.

Human evaluation supports the reported improvement: SFTMix receives 42.5% wins versus 26.5% for NTP across 200 judgments on 80 prompts. Experiments with LoRA, data selection, weaker reference models, and multilingual tuning also demonstrate useful compatibility.
weaknesses: The central contribution is not adequately isolated. There is no comparison against Mixup with unrestricted random pairing on the same dataset. Section 5.2 instead evaluates quality-based pairing on a modified dataset, without testing confidence-based pairing on that dataset. This does not establish that training-dynamics-based partitioning is necessary or better than ordinary Mixup.

Evaluation leaves material uncertainty about the gains. Appendix A.1 explicitly selects hyperparameters using the reported MT-Bench and AlpacaEval-2 results, with no separate validation protocol described. No training-seed variability or confidence intervals are reported; repeating judge evaluations does not measure training variability. Cross-model consistency is encouraging, but these omissions particularly affect interpretation of the smaller improvements.

The proposed mechanism is overstated. Separation of selected confidence extremes in t-SNE and a 7% reduction in confidence-score standard deviation do not demonstrate reduced overfitting or improved generalization specifically for low-confidence examples. Section 3.4 establishes that Mixup changes gradients, but does not explain why confidence-based pairing improves them. Held-out analyses stratified by confidence would substantiate these claims.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the useful high-level description. The manuscript does not provide an implementation link or specify reference-checkpoint locations, input templates, maximum sequence length, precise generation and judge configurations, or LoRA settings. The human evaluation also lacks annotator allocation, agreement, and response-order randomization details.

The practical advantage remains insufficiently characterized. SFTMix requires an additional reference-model training stage and checkpoint scoring, but reports neither total computational overhead nor comparisons under equal compute budgets. Comparisons with inexpensive regularizers such as the cited NEFTune and clearer differentiation from prior cartography-based Mixup would strengthen the contribution. The breadth of positive results makes Findings plausible, but the missing central control and evaluation details prevent a clear positive recommendation.
